  "passage_text": "PREFACE

The history of Gnosticism, which may be defined as the belief that man’s
place in the next world is determined by the knowledge of it that he
acquires in this, goes back probably to the very dawn of our
civilisation; but its importance for most of us is mainly centred round
the first three centuries of our Era. Not even Christianity, as
Amélineau quotes from Pascal, was able at once to make an angel out of a
beast; and no sooner did it emerge from its first home in Judæa into the
broader light of the Roman Empire than there sprang up within it many
more or less secret schools which sought to combine the truths of the
new religion with some of the most pernicious superstitions of the old.
Until lately, however, our knowledge of the teaching of these
post-Christian Gnostics has been limited to the statements of their
opponents. Before the close of the second century, Irenaeus and
Tertullian had written against them; and, some two hundred years later,
Epiphanius, then Bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, repeated their
accusations in his huge _Panarion_, with some doubtful additions of his
own in a form which at least has the merit of restoring for us a great
part of the lost Greek text of Irenaeus. These writers were avowed
heresy-hunters, keenly alive to the danger to Christianity in the
doctrines which they exposed, and therefore necessarily inclined to
believe the worst that could be said against them. But granting the
Fathers’ entire good faith in the matter—and that of Irenaeus and
Tertullian at least is undoubted—there was one cogent reason why their
account of Gnostic teaching had to be received with suspicion. The
leaders of the Gnostics did not teach openly but in secret and by a
method of initiation and allegory which was directly copied from the
Mysteries then current in the Pagan world; and such of their writings as
fell into the hands of the Catholics were therefore not likely to give
any clear view of their doctrine without prolonged study and comparison.
Hence the heresiologists, while dwelling upon minor points which seemed
strange and absurd to those who had not the key to their meaning,
exaggerated the differences between the different teachers and ignored
for the most part the many features of their teaching which they had in
common. In the words of one who certainly had no leaning towards the
error which the Fathers belabour: “... they took minor and unimportant
details and magnified them, and treated them as the essentials of a
system or systems.... The essential principles were largely the same
throughout, the difference was chiefly in regard to details. It is this
conduct on the part of the Fathers that gives us such a distorted and
often ridiculous view of Gnosticism.”[1]

It is true that Clement of Alexandria and his friend Origen, writing in
the birthplace of post-Christian Gnosticism, afford us a more tolerant
and philosophical idea of Gnostical teaching, and have even preserved
for us some precious extracts from the writings of the school of
Valentinus, the great leader—who at one time nearly attained to the
Primacy of the Catholic Church; but save for this, it was not until the
middle of the nineteenth century that we had any chance of studying
Gnosticism from the works of its adherents. The discovery in 1840 of an
almost complete copy of Hippolytus’ _Philosophumena_ gave us for the
first time sufficient excerpts from those writings to enable us to judge
of their style and form; and the publication in 1851 of Schwartze’s text
of the _Pistis Sophia_ first made it known to the world of scholars that
there were in the Museums of London and Oxford Coptic MSS. undoubtedly
written by Gnostics for Gnostics. It is the longer and more important of
these which forms the subject of the following pages.

The value of our text for the study of the early days of Christianity
can hardly be overrated. If I am right in my conclusions, the main part
of the documents which it contains are actually from the school of
Valentinus, the heresiarch just mentioned who flourished in the reign of
Hadrian and Antoninus Pius, and one of them was certainly written before
the Fourth Gospel was known to the Christian communities of the East.
Hence it is to be placed among the earliest Christian writings, and
follows immediately in point of date on the Synoptics and other writings
of the Apostolic Age. Both this and the other documents in the MS. show
also how these heretical schools used to wring and twist Scripture for
their purpose, how closely their teaching was linked with the Egyptian
and other religions of the pre-Christian world, and how surely, in spite
of some good and even noble elements, it was bound to end as they did in
what the late Professor Tylor styled with justice “one of the most
pernicious delusions which ever vexed mankind, the belief in magic.” As
I am dealing with this at more length in the Introduction, I will say
nothing further about it here; but I may point out that the outlandish
names and words in the later documents of our text have not yet been
fully elucidated, and that it is probable that many of its episodes are
intended to bear an allegorical interpretation. The use of words in a
double sense is also one of the many means adopted by the writers in
order to conceal their meaning from the profane, and this should be
constantly borne in mind by the reader."

THE FIFTH DOCUMENT ... 193

INDEX OF PSALMS AND ODES ... 201

GENERAL INDEX ... 203

                              INTRODUCTION

                   1. THE MANUSCRIPT AND ITS HISTORY

The Manuscript known as the _Pistis Sophia_ and now in the British
Museum was bought by the authorities in 1785 for the sum of ten guineas
at the sale of the library of the antiquary, Dr. Anthony Askew. How it
came into Dr. Askew’s possession is not accurately known. It is written
throughout in Coptic of the dialect of the Sahid or Upper Egypt, and is
on vellum in an excellent state of preservation. In appearance it
singularly resembles a modern book, being written on small quarto leaves
measuring 8⅜ inches by 6½, in double columns on both sides of the skins.
It contains 174 leaves in all, and the pages are numbered consecutively
in Coptic[2] letters, at first on one side of the page only, but later
on both sides. We are therefore able to establish that there are no
leaves missing from the body of the MS. since its pagination, until we
come to the 337th page (p. 379 of Schwartze’s printed text),[3] after
which four leaves are wanting, the next page in the volume being
numbered 344. On the 114th page (p. 125 of Schwartze), the scribe had
left the last two-thirds of the page blank, and this was filled at some
later time by the cryptogram given on p. 62, _infra_, in a different
hand and in blacker ink than the foregoing part of the MS. The original
writing is resumed on p. 115, but above the point at which the other
pages begin is written:

“The Second Tome of the Pistis Sophia,” from which the whole MS. has
taken the title by which it is known. At the foot of the first column of
the front or _recto_ of p. 233 (p. 252 of Schwartze), there is also
written after a line of ornament,

“A part of the Books of the Saviour,” and the same words (omitting one
word) occur at the foot of the first column of the back or _verso_ of p.
317 (p. 357 of Schwartze). On the last leaf in the book has been left a
blank, which some later writer has used for a sentence about the
Apostles going to the four quarters of the world to preach the Gospel,
which has no apparent connection with our text.[4] Two lines at the
foot, now become so faint as to be illegible, may have contained the
names of the scribes or owners of the MS.

Apart from this incidental use of the parchment on which it is written,
all who have studied the MS. are of opinion that it is the work of more
than one scribe. Uncial letters are used throughout, and for the first
score or so of pages are so carefully and elegantly formed as to compare
not unfavourably with those of the calligraphically perfect _Codex
Alexandrinus_, also on exhibition in the British Museum. According to
Mr. Crum, whose acquaintance with nearly every Coptic MS. yet brought to
light is unrivalled, the second hand begins at the twenty-second page,
after which the writing not only becomes more careless and the letters
less well formed, but the method of correction for misspelt or omitted
words alters. This second hand continues, according to the same
authority, up to p. 210, when the first hand resumes and continues up to
p. 386, but Mr. Crum says nothing as to the writing of the few remaining
pages. Dr. Carl Schmidt of Berlin, whose work in connection with the MS.
will be noticed at length later, agrees in the main with this, and would
apparently put the termination of the second scribe’s task at p. 195 of
the manuscript, and he says that the first scribe here resumes and
continues to the end. A note, however, taken by the present writer on
his first inspection of the MS. thirty years ago, records that while the
writing of the Second Document, which begins at p. 125, on the whole
resembles the writing of the preceding pages, yet a change takes place
on the _verso_ of p. 210 which indicates yet a third hand, and this is
confirmed by his later scrutiny for the purpose of this edition.[5] Save
for this, there is no serious doubt as to the number of hands which have
worked on the MS.; and Mr. Crum, in confirming Dr. Schmidt’s view that
the alternative work of the scribes shows that the whole of the MS. must
have been written at one time, adds that the corrections of the work of
the second scribe seem to be in the hand-writing of the first.[6] This
is of importance when we come to consider the purpose with which the MS.
was made.

The date at which the MS. was written is the subject of a much greater
difference of opinion. Woide, who was the first to call attention to it,
thought that this was at latest the fourth century, the Abbé Hyvernat
the seventh,[7] Amélineau—whose work upon it will presently be
noticed—the ninth or tenth, and Dr. Schmidt the fifth. All these
conclusions were apparently arrived at on paleographic grounds and I do
not feel myself qualified to discuss them; but the dates of the
different documents from which the MS. was copied will be dealt with
later. Nearly all those who have studied it are of opinion that these
documents were originally written in Greek, and that our MS. is
therefore only a translation.[8]"

The learned\nAcademician, Dulaurier, when on a visit to England, in 1838, also made a\ncopy of our MS., and proposed to publish it with a French translation,\nbut died before doing so; and the MS. would probably have remained\nunknown even to scholars but for the pains of Maurice George Schwartze,\na young German, who was sent over here in 1848 by the generosity of the\nKing of Prussia, to study such of our MSS. as seemed to him valuable.\nSchwartze completed a fairly accurate copy of the text, and also\ntranslated it into Latin retaining untranslated the Greek words which\noccur on every page; but he too died before the result of his labours\ncould be printed, and the task of editing and correcting his translation\nfell upon his friend Petermann, who published both Schwartze’s Coptic\ntext and his Latin (and Greek) translation in 1853. Unfortunately,\nPetermann, though a competent Coptic scholar for his time, did not feel\ncalled upon to contribute anything more than textual criticism to his\npredecessor’s work.[9] Schwartze’s text was therefore published without\nintroduction or notes other than corrections of mistranslated words and\nsuggestions for alternative readings; and this prevented the book from\nobtaining such general notice as was given to the _Philosophumena_ of\nHippolytus which appeared at nearly the same time. Bunsen, who had begun\nthe controversy between Catholic and Protestant scholars which sprang up\nround Hippolytus’ work,[10] poured contempt upon the _Pistis Sophia_ as\n“a most worthless offshoot of the Marcosian heresy,” and, although\nKöstlin contributed a long discussion of the work to a Tübingen\ntheological annual in 1854,[11] it remained practically unknown to\nEnglish readers for more than thirty years.[12]\n\nAt length in 1887, Lipsius published a detailed study of it in Smith and\nWace’s _Dictionary of Christian Biography_, in which full use was made\nof Köstlin’s analysis, and he agreed with that writer in assigning to it\nan Ophite origin, although he also drew attention to certain\npeculiarities which appeared to him Manichæan. In the same year there\nalso appeared the second edition of C. W. King’s _Gnostics and their\nRemains_, which gave for the first time to English readers translations\nof a great part of the work. The late Mr. King, then Senior Fellow of\nTrinity College, Cambridge, had hitherto been known chiefly as a\ncollector of ancient gems on which he had published many useful volumes,\nand he proposed, like his predecessors, to publish a full translation of\nthe _Pistis Sophia_. At his death such a translation was found among his\npapers; but the failure of his eyesight, which had taken place even\nbefore the issue of the second edition of his _Gnostics_, had left it in\nsuch a condition that his executors decided against giving it to the\npublic. It was confessedly made from Schwartze’s Græco-Latin version\nonly; but Mr. King did much to attract public notice to the _Pistis\nSophia_ by the excellent and dignified English in which his extracts\nfrom it were clothed, and the erudition which he brought to bear upon\npoints like the less-known religions of the Roman Empire and the\nbarbarous names and words left entirely unexplained in Schwartze’s\nversion. He also asserted in his Preface, with much show of reason, that\nit was the statements made by him in his first edition that led Madame\nBlavatsky, whom he describes as “the Sibyl of Esoteric Buddhism,” to\ninclude the relics of Gnosticism among the foundations of what he refers\nto as “her new religion.”"
}

  "passage_text": "Before this hint was taken, the MS. again received attention from a\nscholar in many respects well fitted to deal with it. M. Amélineau, who\nhad for many years devoted himself to the study of Coptic religious\ntexts, and had also a very considerable working knowledge of Egyptology,\npublished in the same year of 1887, in the _Annales du Musée Guimet_ an\n“Essai sur le Gnosticisme Egyptien,” in which he dealt at great length\nwith the _Pistis Sophia_, and compared it for the first time to the\n_Papyrus Bruce_ of the Bodleian Library at Oxford which had hitherto\ndefied interpretation. Both these works he assigned to the school of\nValentinus, the heresiarch whom the Ante-Nicene Fathers considered the\nmost dangerous enemy of the Catholic Church, and he followed this up in\n1891 by publishing in the _Notices et Extraits_ of the Académie des\nInscriptions, the text and translation into French of the Oxford\nPapyrus. These two publications were both made at the expense of the\nFrench Government and were therefore produced in a style worthy of the\nsubject, and with all the notes, references, and illustrations that they\nseemed to demand. But the _Pistis Sophia_ remained untouched by M.\nAmélineau save for the excerpts from it to be found in his _Essai_,\nuntil in 1895 he astonished the learned world by publishing in a series\ncalled “_Les Classiques de l’Occulte_,” a low-priced translation into\nFrench of the whole _Pistis Sophia_ with a comparatively brief\nintroduction devoted almost entirely to the vindication of the opinion\nformerly advanced by him as to its authorship. M. Amélineau will be\nremembered by many as the first explorer of the Protodynastic Tombs at\nAbydos which entirely revolutionised all our ideas of early Egyptian\nhistory; and it was probably only the difficulties under which he\nlaboured all his life which prevented him from publishing the results of\nthis—his first and only excavation—in a manner which would have gained\nhim the full credit of his really epoch-making discovery.[13] It was\ndoubtless the same difficulties which compelled him to produce his\ntranslation of the _Pistis Sophia_ in the form in which he did; and\nalthough he states in his Introduction that he inspected the MS. at the\nBritish Museum during a visit to London shortly before his translation\nappeared, it is plain that this translation was made from Schwartze’s\ntext only, that the work was executed throughout in so hasty a fashion\nas to leave nearly all the faults of Schwartze’s version uncorrected,\nand that it passes by most of the difficulties presented by the MS.\nwithout attempt at solution. It was in consequence very severely\ncriticised first by Dr. Schmidt, and then by Dr. Andersson, the editor\nof the Swedish Egyptological periodical, _Sphinx_, and most of these\ncriticisms appear unfortunately to be well founded.\n\nSuch as it was, however, it gave rise to the only complete English\ntranslation of our MS. which has yet appeared in print. Mr. G. R. S.\nMead, then secretary of the Theosophical Society, the year after the\nappearance of Amélineau’s French translation, published with the\nTheosophical Publishing Company an English translation of the _Pistis\nSophia_, which on its title-page is expressed to be made from\n“Schwartze’s Latin Version ... checked by Amélineau’s French Version.”\nMr. Mead laid no claims to proficiency in Coptic, and had already\npublished more than half his work in a Theosophical magazine before\nAmélineau’s version saw the light. His attitude towards the original may\nbe guessed by the statement in his Preface that the comprehensive\ntreatment of Gnosticism “requires not only a writer who at least\nbelieves in the possibilities of magic, but also a mystic or at least a\nperson who is in sympathy with mysticism,” and by the fact that he had\nalready attempted to explain the Cabalistic Cryptogram on p. 125 by\nSanskrit words. He further states in his Introduction that he proposes\nto publish a commentary on the whole book, his Introduction dealing only\nwith the date and authorship; but up to the present this has not\nappeared. It is also evident that in his translation from Schwartze’s\nLatin version he has omitted in more than one instance to notice\nPetermann’s emendations, which in some cases completely change the\nmeaning of the passage; and altogether it may be said that the most\nvaluable part of his work is the short bibliography appended, in which\nhe gives fairly long extracts from the authors whom he quotes."

  "passage_text": "The way was therefore still left open for a translation of the _Pistis
Sophia_ by competent hands, and the appearance of Dr. Schmidt’s work in
1905 at first sight gave hopes that this was at last accomplished. The
book, which bears the somewhat clumsy title of _Koptisch-Gnostischen
Schriften, Ersten Buch_ only, is one of the excellent series of
translations of Christian writers of the first three centuries published
by the Church Fathers Committee of the Royal Prussian Academy of
Science, and contains a full German translation of both the _Pistis
Sophia_ and the _Bruce Papyrus_. Dr. Schmidt is a scholar whose
competence in the Coptic language is probably only surpassed by that of
Mr. Crum, he has all his’ countrymen’s taste for philology and grammar,
and his acquaintance with the Christian literature of the early
centuries of our Era is profound. It is not therefore to be wondered at
that his translation of our text is from the etymological point of view
as nearly perfect as our present knowledge of Coptic—still limited by
the paucity of MSS. other than Biblical—allows it to be, and that very
little complaint can be made against it on the score of verbal accuracy.
The addition to it of a translation of the _Bruce Papyrus_ is also most
convenient for purposes of reference; but perhaps by reason of this, Dr.
Schmidt’s notes on his translation of the British Museum MS. are
confined to Scripture references and verbal matters only, while in his
Introduction he only gives seventeen pages to consideration of its
history, writing, language, composition, source, and date. This cursory
treatment is doubtless in part due to his having in the text and
translation of the _Bruce Papyrus_, published by him in 1892 in Harnack
and Gebhardt’s well-known series of “_Texte und Untersuchungen_,”
already given his views on these matters, most of which he reiterates in
the Introduction last mentioned. These views may be briefly stated as
follows:

    1. The _Pistis Sophia_ is not Valentinian, but comes from an obscure
    sect of what he calls Barbelo-Gnostics, known as Severiani.

    2. Its title should not be _Pistis Sophia_ but Τεύχη τοῦ Σωτῆρος.

    3. While admitting that the whole work is a
    “_Miszellenhandschrift_,” he thinks that the Fourth Document is the
    oldest in the collection and, as it were, the root of the other
    three, which in their turn form a connected whole.

Dr. Schmidt’s fellow-countrymen Drs. Lichtenhau and Preuschen have
already attacked some of these positions in the _Zeitschrift für
wissenschaftliche Theologie_[14] and elsewhere, and after mature
consideration, the present writer feels himself compelled to dissent
from all three. The reasons for doing so will be best given when we come
to consider the composition and authorship of the MS. Before leaving
this branch of the subject, however, it may be said that beside the work
of Köstlin, Lipsius, and Dr. Schmidt, the _Pistis Sophia_ has been
treated of at some length in Father Giraud’s _Ophitus_ (1884), and in a
special work by Prof. Harnack in the _Texte und Untersuchungen_ above
mentioned (1891). More recently, it has also been dealt with by M.
Eugène de Faye in his _Introduction à l’Etude du Gnosticisme_ (1903) and
his _Gnostiques et Gnosticisme_ (1913), by Dr. James Moffat in his
article under its name in Hastings’ _Encyclopædia of Religion and
Ethics_, and by the present writer in his _Forerunners and Rivals of
Christianity_ (1915).[15] The late Sir Gaston Maspero and Prof. Lieblein
(of Christiania) have also stated their conviction that it could only
have been written by persons intimately acquainted with the old Egyptian
religion, on which point none could speak with greater authority than
they.[16]

                      2. THE DOCUMENTS IN THE MS.

As has been said above, Dr. Schmidt speaks of our text as a miscellany,
and the phrase by no means overstates the case. It contains indeed no
less than six documents, only the two first of which are directly
connected or can be taken as necessarily intended to be read
consecutively. The second of these breaks off in the middle of a
conversation, the third has neither beginning nor end. The opening
sentence of the fourth implies that it is the continuation of a
conversation which cannot be certainly identified with any that has gone
before, and the same document concludes with a sentence which does not
seem likely to be the end of the extract. The fifth begins with what is
clearly a fresh narrative without reference to anything that has
preceded it and must have ended in the _lacuna_ caused by the missing
pages, while the sixth, whose beginning has been lost in the same
_lacuna_, ends in the middle of a phrase. Of these six documents, the
third only covers one and a half pages of the MS. and is manifestly a
fragment of some document which has somehow strayed over into this
place; but as it appears directly after the words: “A Part of the Books
of the Saviour,” I hesitate to say that it never formed part of any of
the other documents in the text, and I shall therefore speak of it
hereafter as “The Interpolated Fragment” merely. Only the two first of
the six, also, can claim to be included under the title of the _Pistis
Sophia_, but they are by far the largest and take up between them more
than half the volume. This arrangement follows strictly the rule of
stichometry observed by writers of the period, which prescribes that the
longest document shall come first. Thus in this translation:—

                  Document       Begin page   End page
                  1st                    63        126
                  2nd                    63        126
                  Interpolated          127        128
                  3rd                   128        179
                  4th                   180        192
                  5th                   193        199

Taking these in this order, we will summarise them as briefly as
possible."
}

The FIRST DOCUMENT, then, tells how Jesus spent twelve years after the
Resurrection teaching His disciples the mysteries of the heavenly
“places,”[17] but that their instruction did not extend beyond this
visible, or more accurately, this sensible, universe which corresponds,
it would seem, to the Third Chorema or Space of the “First Mystery” or
God Manifest, of Whom Jesus is the Incarnation. This Chorema is under
the governance of a Power called the First Law, under whom are eleven
others called the Five Marks, the Great Light, and the Five Parastatai
or Helpers; and all these twelve came from still higher states of being
from which, we are told later, they voluntarily descended to take part
in the scheme of salvation. When the First Document opens, however,
Jesus has only told His disciples of the existence of those Powers, but
has not revealed to them their origin, function, or arrangement; and all
the action in this Document passes in the lower part of this Chorema
which is called the Kerasmos or Confusion, because in it Light is
mingled with Matter. The highest part of the Kerasmos is the Treasure
house where the Light as it is won from Matter is stored up; and then
come a great number of inferior Places inhabited by Powers concerned
with the administration of our universe’s more material parts,
especially the heavenly bodies or sun, moon, and stars. Below these
again is our earth with its firmament or “Height,” and outside this
Chaos or the dark and unformed mass of Matter which has received no
Light.[18]

While Jesus is sitting with His disciples on the Mount of Olives, the
Document goes on to say, there descends upon Him a “Great Power of
Light,” which is in fact the “vesture” or Heavenly Nature which He had
left in the Limit or Lower Boundary of the upper worlds on His descent
to earth in “the shape of Gabriel.” This vesture enables Him to rise to
the Boundary and there assume two other vestures which are necessary for
the continuation of the journey to the two transcendental “Spaces” which
are higher than this. In this first vesture, also, He finds five
mysterious words written which are here interpreted as an address from
the higher powers hailing Him as the First Mystery, and the catalogue of
names which follows enables us to form a fairly correct idea of the
arrangement of this Chorema as well as of the higher ones which are
known as the “Spaces” of the First Mystery and of the “Ineffable” or
Supreme Unmanifested God respectively.[19]

On assuming this vesture, Jesus flies into the Height, but returns the
next day clad in three vestures of dazzling light, and tells His
disciples how He provided for the births of Himself and them by casting
into their respective mothers Powers from the higher parts of the
Kerasmos instead of the material souls which they would otherwise have
received from the Rulers of the stars. In like manner also, He tells how
He caused the soul of Elijah to become incarnate in the body of John the
Baptist. He then goes on to describe His journey upward through the
First Sphere directly above the firmament, the Second Sphere called
Destiny, and the Twelve Æons,[20] which appear to be the signs of the
Zodiac. The Kings or Tyrants of these last rebel against Him, and He
punishes them by taking away part of their power and altering their
course, so that mankind will no longer be able to foretell the future by
means of the astrology and magic taught them by the sinning angels.
Leaving their Place, He ascends to the thirteenth Æon, and finds below
it Pistis Sophia, the heroine of the book. She is, it appears, one of
the twenty-four Unseen or Invisible Ones put forth in pairs by the head
of the Left Hand or most material part of the Kerasmos, and had left her
spouse and her work to pursue a light which she saw below her and which
she thought would enable her to mount to the Treasure-house. This light,
however, was a snare sent into Chaos by one of the material Powers
immediately above her; and on her advancing to seize it, she was set
upon by several material Powers that her persecutor had put forth and
deprived of her own light, so that she could not return to her own Place
in the thirteenth Æon.

In this plight, she sings hymns of penitence to the “Light of Lights” or
Light of the Treasure-house, and these are all recited at full length by
Jesus to His disciples, who identify them at His instance with passages
from the Canonical Psalms, and from those “Odes of Solomon” which are
mentioned above. These Penitences are twelve in number, and in the
course of their recital and the conversation that takes place on them,
we learn something more about the arrangement of the different worlds
and the process of the redemption of Light from Matter which it is
apparently the object of the book to describe. Finally, after this tenth
“Penitence,” Jesus, who has throughout her affliction procured for
Pistis Sophia certain alleviations in her misery, calls into existence
several new Powers who go into Chaos to her assistance and form a crown
of light to her head, so that her tormentors dare not come near to her.

With this the Document ends, and it is manifest from the appearance of
the MS. that the scribes who wrote it, at this point thought that they
had come to the end of their task and did not then expect to carry it
further.

                  *       *       *       *       *"
}

  "passage_text": "The SECOND DOCUMENT begins with the caption “The Second Tome of Pistis
Sophia” in a handwriting which Mr. Crum has no hesitation in declaring
to be the same as that of the first seventy pages of the Document.
Whereas the First Document ends, however, with Jesus’ approval of Mary
Magdalene’s interpretation of the quotation from the Psalms about Mercy
and Truth kissing each other, the Second Document opens with another
interpretation of the same text offered by John. Coupled with the
caption given above, this seems sufficient to show that the Second
Document was intended to be taken for a continuation of the First,
although this by no means proves that they were written at the same time
or by the same author. The Document goes on to elaborate the story of
the rescue of Pistis Sophia, and tells with great detail how Gabriel and
Michael being summoned for that purpose go to her assistance. This
provokes a fresh display of anger on the part of the “Self-willed God”
who is Pistis Sophia’s chief persecutor, and the powers of Chaos make a
fresh assault upon her. On this, Jesus orders Gabriel and Michael to
bear her on their hands out of Chaos, while He Himself descends thither,
smites her tormentors, and renders them powerless to follow her. He then
leads her into the “Place below the thirteenth Æon” where He finds her
on His ascension from the Mount of Olives, and warns her that she will
again be tormented when the Gate of the Treasure-house is set open. This
apparently happens just before Jesus’ ascension in the vesture of light,
and He then routs her enemies for the last time and restores her to her
original Place in the thirteenth Æon, where she sings a final song of
praise to Him for the wonders which He has wrought for her “in the world
of men.”

This ends the episode of Pistis Sophia, who is not again mentioned until
we come to the Fourth Document. The author now turns to what was
probably the main reason for attempting the continuation of the First
Document, which is the questioning of Mary Magdalene and the other
disciples upon the order and use of the Heavenly Places, and the
Saviour’s replies thereto.[21] Beginning with the answer to Mary’s
question as to the nature of the twenty-four Unseen Ones of whom Pistis
Sophia was one, the Saviour promises Himself to lead the disciples
through all the Upper worlds right up to that of the Ineffable One
Himself, each successive world and even Place being, it is said, so
greatly superior in size and in light to the lower ones, that they will
appear like grains of dust when viewed from it. He also tells them that
the beatitudes in store for them will be progressive, beginning with the
Millenium which will ensue when the number of perfect souls is
accomplished, the Kerasmos purified and “caught up,” and the Twelve
Disciples established with Jesus as joint Kings reigning over the
blessed in the Last Parastates or Helper—a name given to the world which
is placed in our universe immediately over the Treasure-house. Here they
will apparently receive further instruction and be given “mysteries”
which will enable them to mount to the upper universes before, it is
expressly said, the “Projections” or emanations of the Treasure-house
who are concerned with the administration of the scheme of salvation.
The details of this scheme are extremely complicated, the Saviour
several times promising to explain further in a subsequent revelation
constantly referred to as “the Distribution of the Universe.”

But its final aim is indicated without ambiguity. Jesus, who as we have
seen was hailed in the First Document as the First Mystery in the
address of the Spirits written on the vesture of light sent to Him on
the Mount of Olives, is throughout this part of the Second Document
always spoken of by that title; and we are told that those who receive
the highest mystery of all, called the “Mystery of the Ineffable One,”
will be absorbed into His being. “That Man is I, and I am that Man,” are
the words in which this announcement is made, and the full meaning of
the phrase can be appreciated by other sentences in the narrative which
go to show that this First Mystery is the first Being to come forth from
the Ineffable One, and is regarded as a “Twin Mystery” or Father and
Son, the first-named or “First Mystery looking inwards” being alone
capable of remaining in contemplation of the greatness of the Ineffable
One, while the Son or “First Mystery looking outwards” is sent to earth
in the Person of Jesus Himself.[22]

The way to obtain this elevation in the scale of being is, perhaps, left
purposely obscure, but it can apparently be gained by certain
initiations or mysteries, which like the Mysteries of Eleusis will give
the initiate the knowledge of the universe, how it came to be, and how
it will end. These also are progressive and culminate in the “One Word
of the Ineffable One,” the effect of which is so tremendous that if it
be spoken over the dying, or for the dead, whether partly initiate or
wholly uninitiate, it will expedite his passage to the heaven to which
his initiation entitles him, or, in the case of one wholly uninitiate,
will ensure his reincarnation in a “righteous” body, which will “find
the God of Truth and the exalted mysteries, and will inherit them and
the Light for ever and ever.”[23] The way to this and to the Mysteries
in general is “the renunciation of the whole world and all the matter
therein.”"

  "passage_text": "Beside this, however, there are lesser mysteries which will admit the\nfaithful recipient to heaven and privileges less exalted indeed than\nthat last described, but will yet confer on him great beatitude after\ndeath. These, known collectively as the “Mysteries of the third Space,”\ninvolve a “Defence” a “Password” and a “Symbol” which have to be handed\nin by the dead in his flight upward so as to procure him uninterrupted\npassage to the heaven of which he has received the mystery. Of these, it\nis said that the disciples have no need, because nothing of the sort is\nrequired by the recipients of the higher mysteries, but Jesus adds that\nthey are to be found in “the two great Books of Jeu” which “Enoch wrote\nwhen I spake with him out of the Tree of Knowledge and the Tree of Life\nin the Paradise of Adam.”[24] In spite of these assurances, Andrew\nprovokes the Saviour by asking how “men of this world” can be expected\nto adventure after death upon the long and dangerous journey among all\nthe Great Powers of the Treasurehouse and their subordinates, and the\nSaviour reminds him in reply that they and He are all of the same\norigin, being made from “the same mass and the same matter and the same\nsubstance” and are all “out of the same Confusion.”[25] On this, the\nother disciples successfully implore Jesus to pardon Andrew, and this\nDocument ends in the middle of a sentence in which He declares that He\nhas been sent for the remission of sins.\n\nBefore leaving this Document, it must be noted that in it there appear\nlong rhetorical statements in a form which has no parallel in the other\ndocuments of our text. They repeat the same phrase with the variation of\ntwo or three words at each repetition, the object being apparently to\ngive the hearer an idea which he could not otherwise obtain—except,\nperhaps, by a picture or diagram[26] of the different hierarchies of\nPowers or arrangement of Places which the speaker is describing. Thus in\none place, Jesus, after speaking of the “Mystery of the Ineffable One,”\ngoes on to declare that “that Mystery knoweth why the Darkness came to\nbe and why the Light,” and then after going through a string of similar\nantitheses in which the Treasurehouse is contrasted with Chaos, murder\nwith the quickening of souls, Death with Life and all sorts of natural\nphenomena with one another, continues with “That Mystery knoweth why the\nTriple Powers came to be and why the Unseen Ones,” and so on through an\nincredible number of Spirits and Powers until He at last reaches the\nFirst Emanation of the Ineffable One which is in fact Himself. This is\namplified when He says later that “That Mystery knoweth” why these\nhigher Powers “despoiled” themselves (or stripped themselves of their\nexalted natures), when a great part of the Places and Powers of the\nhighest worlds are enumerated all over again. Not long after this, He\nhas occasion to speak of the man who receives this same Mystery of the\nIneffable One, when He says that “He is a man in the world, but he\nexcelleth all the Angels and is more excellent than them all,” and then\nrepeats the same phrase with regard to Archangels, Unseen Ones, Triple\nPowers, and all the Projections of the Treasurehouse and its\ndependencies for the third time.[27] This kind of rhapsody does not seem\nto be cast into any rhythmical form, yet seems to be intended for\nrepetition by word of mouth rather than by writing. The only likeness\nthat I can find to this practice is in one of the Chapters of the _Book\nof the Dead_, where all the different parts of the Hall of Two Truths\ndemand to be told their names, or those in the _Book of Gates_ where the\nparts of the Bark of Ra make the like demand. It therefore seems to be a\npurely Egyptian feature and may be connected with the fact that the\nearly Egyptian Church, like the colleges formed for the worship of gods\nlike Amen in earlier times, had “prophets,” who seem to have occupied a\nposition in the Church next after the bishop.\n\n                  *       *       *       *       *\n\nThe INTERPOLATED FRAGMENT which occupies most of the first leaf of the\nThird Document is entirely taken up with the relation of the Ineffable\none to His “members”; but is too short and disconnected to give us much\ninformation on the subject. It is put into the mouth of Jesus and it\nmakes allusion to other revelations which Jesus is said to have\npreviously made or “written,” or which He promises. The style is not\nunlike that of the First Document, so that I do not see why it may not\nbe an extract from the same book if, as may be probable, Jesus continued\nin it the account of His upward journey after leaving Pistis Sophia in\nthe thirteenth Æon.[28]\n\n                  *       *       *       *       *"

  "passage_text": "The THIRD DOCUMENT may perhaps be called without fear of contradiction\n“Part of the Books of the Saviour,” because it bears that title both at\nits head and at its foot. It begins by an exhortation to the disciples\nto preach “to the whole world” a series of ἀποτάγματα or renunciations\nof sin which may be connected with Jesus’ speech to Andrew at the end of\nthe Second Document. It should be noted, however, that while in the\nSecond Document mankind is to be entreated to renounce the world and its\nmatter so that they may “go unto the Light,” the author of this Document\npresses them to abjure sin lest they suffer the torments of hell. These\ntorments are also dealt with in considerable detail, and we can gather\nfrom the description that there are four Places of Punishment called\nrespectively Amente, Chaos, the Middle Way, and the Outer Darkness.[29]\nThis seems to be a sort of amalgam of different traditional beliefs, for\nwhile Amente appears in the _Book of the Dead_, Chaos in the First\nDocument does not seem to be thought of as necessarily a Place of\nPunishment, and we have seen Pistis Sophia speaking of it in the Second\nDocument as “the world of men.” So, too, the location of these different\nhells shows some confusion of thought. Amente is probably in the West or\nbeyond the earth as it is in the _Book of the Dead_, Chaos is either the\nearth itself or beneath it, while the Middle Way is, like the Place of\nPunishment in the Enochian literature, in the firmament or “below the\nSphere.” As for the Outer Darkness, its name shows it to be a relic of\nPagan Egypt where it was held that beyond the confines of the earth, the\nair became so thick as to be actually tangible and concrete. Among the\ntormentors in these various hells we find Ariel, Pistis Sophia’s\npersecutor Ialdabaoth, one “Iakhthanabas the Merciless” and the Dragon\nof Outer Darkness who is depicted as a great serpent coiled round the\nworld having his tail in his mouth and containing places of torment\nwithin him where ice and cold come to supplement the tortures of fire\nand smoke.\n\nA great part of the Document is likewise taken up by the questions of\nMary Magdalene and the other disciples, among whom John is the most\ninsistent, as to the sinners to whom they shall give their mysteries and\nthe effect which they will have on them. We who hear in this Document of\na mystery or secret whereby the dead can be raised, the sick healed, and\nother wonders performed, although Jesus tells His disciples that this\nmystery belongs to the Archons or wicked Rulers of the Stars and is not\nto be used save for the purpose of establishing the faith throughout the\nworld.[30] We also have much in this Document as to the soul or\nincorporeal part of man which the disciples are told consists of the\nPower, the Soul proper, the Spirit Counterfeit, and the Fate. Of these,\nthe Power is the most worthy and causes the man to seek after the\nmysteries, and the soul is really the Life or Breath and is made either\nout of the _ejecta_ of the Rulers or from the dregs or grosser parts of\nthe Light which is at certain periods squeezed out of them by certain\npowers appointed for that purpose. The Spirit Counterfeit, on the other\nhand, is the envelope or mask of the soul which constantly leads it to\ncommit sin and bears witness after death to its having done so, while\nthe Fate is the death to which the man is predestined, and which he can\nnever escape while uninitiate.[31] Incidentally, too, we hear a good\ndeal in this Document as to the Gnostic belief in the transmigration of\nsouls, reincarnation being obligatory on such souls as have not found\nthe more sublime mysteries.[32] Several formulas are also given whereby\nthe soul can cut itself loose from the Spirit Counterfeit and the Fate,\nand we are told that even an uninitiated person can escape from the\ntorments of the Dragon of Outer Darkness if one of the names of the\nreptile be said by or for him. Throughout this Document the tortures of\nthe different hells and the beast-shaped demons who administer them are\nmuch dwelt upon. Finally, Jesus tells His disciples that He came to\nearth to bring these mysteries, and that had He not done so neither\nPatriarchs nor Prophets would have entered into the Light.[33]\n\n                  *       *       *       *       *"
}

  "passage_text": "The opening sentence of the FOURTH DOCUMENT shows plainly that it comes
from a book written independently of the preceding ones and not as their
continuation. It ignores completely the tradition held in the time of
the Antonines by orthodox and heretic alike, that Jesus spent many years
on earth after the Resurrection,[34] and announces that after He “rose
from among the dead the third day,” His disciples gathered round Him
reminding Him that they had left the whole world to follow Him.[35] Then
begins a scene that reminds one irresistibly of the magical practices
rife during the first three centuries of our Era, some details of which
have come down to us in the _Philosophumena_ and in the different Magic
Papyri to be found in the Museums of Paris, London, Leyden, and Berlin.
Jesus, standing by an altar by the side of the sea “Ocean,” makes
invocation to His Father in words which are not gibberish, as at first
sight they appear to be, but a jumble of Hebrew, Egyptian, and perhaps
Persian words copied and re-copied by scribes ignorant of these
languages until they are all but unrecognisable. He calls upon the name
of the Father of the Treasurehouse of Light, whereupon the heavens open
revealing the “true shapes” of the sun and moon, and Jesus and His
disciples are uplifted to “the Middle Way which is below the Sphere.”
Here the arrangement of the stars is explained to them and they learn
that the rebellious Rulers who persisted in copulation were bound to the
Sphere to the number of 1800 for each sign of the Zodiac, under the rule
of 360 of that number, who are themselves under the sway of the five
Planets, Saturn, Mars, Mercury, Venus, and Jupiter. Yet the author of
this Document must have known, although he varies, the tradition of the
First Document, for Jesus tells His hearers that these planets were
strengthened by the infusion into Saturn of a Power from the Great
Unseen God who projected Pistis Sophia, into Mars of a similar Power
from one of the three Triple-powered Gods, into Mercury of one from
another of the Triple Powers, and into Venus of one from “Pistis Sophia
the daughter of Barbelo”[36]; while one from the “Little Sabaoth the
Good,” a Power of higher rank than these last, who in the story of
Pistis Sophia proper is described as supplying the Power which takes the
place of Jesus’ own earthly soul, is cast into the planet Jupiter and is
given rule over all the others. All these planets are given barbarous
names in addition to their Greek ones, as are the Great Unseen God and
the two Triple Powers, these last names appearing also in the Magic
Papyri, while the names of both planets and Powers appear to have a real
meaning.

Jesus then shows to His disciples the five torture-chambers of the
Middle Way, each of them presided over by an “Authority,” who with his
(or her) assistants has been chosen from among the rebellious Rulers.
Each of these Authorities sees to the punishment of particular sins,
which sins his or her ministers have “entered into man” and caused him
to commit. Three of these presiding demons are females, one of them
being the triple-faced Hecate still famous in the Middle Ages and
Renaissance, and among them we find the merciless Iakhthanabas already
mentioned in the Third Document, and the Egyptian God Typhon. The
different terms of punishment from 150 years downwards which sinful
souls will suffer in these tortures of the Middle Way are all given, and
it is expressly said that these places of torment will be dissolved when
the two beneficent planets, Venus and Jupiter, come into certain
positions in the Zodiac.[37] These Places are, it would seem, actually
shown to the disciples, Jesus thereby in part fulfilling the promise
made in the First Document to lead them through all the heavenly Places.
He then restores the heavens to their normal condition, and returns with
the disciples to the “Mountain of Galilee,” where he celebrates for them
a sacrament with “fire and water, wine and blood.” The distribution of
bread also forms part of this sacrament, and it is accompanied by a
“sign” which we know from other sources was the conversion of one of the
cups of wine into the water of baptism.[38] This “mystery” or sacrament
is said to have the effect of remitting all the sins of the disciples,
and they are told to perform the same ceremony for all those who will
listen to their preaching. They remind Him that there are other Baptisms
of Fire and the Holy Spirit of Light respectively, and He tells them
that these are more excellent than any Mystery save only those of the
Seven Sounds and of the Great Name of God, which if spoken to any demon
will destroy him with all his tortures. He is apparently about to
perform these for the benefit of the disciples when the Document
abruptly ends with the gap left by the tearing-away of the four pages
already noticed.

It must be noted that nearly all the first part of this Document is full
of invocations or prayers couched in the apparent gibberish before
mentioned, that “Mary”—whether the Mother of Jesus or the Magdalene is
not stated—asks one question only, that the planet Venus is called
“Bubastis,” Egyptian, Greek, and Hebrew magic and astrology being
present in nearly every line, while there is some little trace of
Persian influence as well. It is also closely connected with one of the
documents of the _Bruce Papyrus_, where the peculiar sacrament here
celebrated by Jesus is described on similar lines and is followed by the
celebration of the other already mentioned; while in another Document of
the same Papyrus the name of Pistis Sophia is given in connection with a
place of repentance. The story of the Samaritan woman and of the spear
thrust at the Crucifixion is also mentioned in this Fourth Document,
these being the first unmistakable quotations from the Fourth Gospel to
be found in our text.

                  *       *       *       *       *"
}

  "passage_text": "The FIFTH DOCUMENT is, as has been said above, the shortest of all, and\nhas lost its title in the gap of four leaves in the British Museum MS.\nIt is entirely concerned with the punishments assigned to different\nsins; and as sedition, lust, and robbery with violence appear in the\nFourth Document as sins punishable in the Middle Way, but are not\nmentioned in the present fragment, we may presume that they were dealt\nwith in the part lacking, and probably occupied at least three of the\nmissing pages. But the Baptism of Fire and the Holy Spirit which Jesus\nis going to celebrate when the _lacuna_ occurs, if treated at the same\nlength as in the _Bruce Papyrus_, can hardly have taken up less than the\nother five missing pages, and it is therefore plain that nothing in\naddition to these punishments can have occupied the missing beginning of\nthis Document. After this the Fifth Document begins with a broken\nsentence containing the punishment of the man who curses, and then goes\non to describe the punishment of the evil speaker, the murderer, the\nhabitual thief, the proud man, the blasphemer, the sodomite, and the\ncelebrant of the filthy parody of the Eucharist known as the Black\nMass.[39] In one or other of those cases, the four hells of Amente,\nChaos, the Middle Way, and the Outer Darkness are introduced, the\npunishments in them being successive, and we read again here the names\nof Ariel and Ialdabaoth who are mentioned in the Third Document, as\nthose of torturers in Amente and Chaos respectively. So, too, we hear\nagain of the cup of forgetfulness which in the Third Document is\nadministered to the soul after it has been shown the punishments in\norder that it may profit nothing on reincarnation by its knowledge of\ntheir terrors. But here the punishments are so different from those\nformerly described that we see at once we are dealing with a different\nauthor. The sum total of the periods of punishment for cursing which are\nadministered in all the different hells does not amount to more than\nfour years as against the 133 assigned to it in the Fourth Document; and\nthe penalty for slander is here given as no more than 30 years as\nagainst the same period of 133. The Receiver of Sabaoth Adamas, leader\nof the rebellious Rulers, now administers the cup of oblivion instead of\nas in the Third Document, the “Rulers of the head of the Æons,” and he\nis given the name of Ialuham, while the Receivers of Ariel, who are here\nmentioned for the first time in our text, are named Abiuth and Kharmon.\nThe case of the uninitiated but righteous dead is also dealt with in\nanswer to a question from John, but in a different manner from its\ntreatment in the Third Document, as here the soul on coming out of the\nbody is met by the Receivers of Bainkhookh or the planet Mercury, while\nthe cup which takes away the baleful effect of the cup of oblivion is\nadministered by a Receiver of the planet Jupiter[40]. It is also to be\nnoted that in this Document for the first time the division of mankind\ninto “righteous” and “wicked” bodies, which find or do not find, as the\ncase may be, the mysteries of light, is made to depend entirely on the\nperiodic disposition of the stars. When, it is said, the two beneficent\nplanets Jupiter and Venus come before the Virgin of Light and the two\nmaleficent Saturn and Mars behind her in the revolution of the Sphere,\nall the souls sent into the world will be good, and when the position is\nreversed, all will be wicked.[41] Here, too, for the first time, we are\ntold that the form of the body on reincarnation depends on the sins\ncommitted by the soul in its last life,—that the soul of the proud man\nwill be put into a body dumb and deformed, the soul of the thief into\none lame and maimed and blind—and so on.\n\nIt will therefore be seen that this Document is sufficiently connected\nwith some of the preceding ones to warrant the supposition that it comes\nfrom the same school or sect, although it is noteworthy that neither in\nour Fourth nor our Fifth Document are the Ineffable One or the First\nMystery ever referred to. The chief point in common between this Fifth\nDocument and the _Bruce Papyrus_ is the mention of the Black Mass which\nappears in both Documents. A feature peculiar to this Document alone is\nthe open reference to the Pagan Gods as fiends; and besides Typhon and\nHecate, who have in truth a more or less malevolent character in the\nlater Egyptian and Greek mythology, Adonis, one of the forms under which\nOsiris was worshipped at Alexandria, is made to take the soul of the\nthief to Amente, while “the high goddess” of Homer, Persephone, the\nmuch-loved daughter of the Eleusinian Demeter, figures as one of the\ntormentors in Chaos. The sentence about the journeys of the Apostles\nwritten on the blank leaf bound in with the rest of the volume has no\nperceptible connection with our text and may possibly be the work of\nsome one who, suddenly coming across it in some other document and\nwishing to preserve it, seized upon this leaf as the only piece of\nparchment available.\n\n                  *       *       *       *       *"

Lacau and Sir Ernest Wallis Budge from the MSS. in the\n_Bibliothèque Nationale_ and the British Museum respectively. PURPOSE AND COMPOSITION OF THE MS.\n\nWhy now was this miscellany made? Not certainly for edification or the\nuse of the sect or school[42] whose doctrines it sets forth. Every\nCoptic inscription on tombstone or wall and nearly every Coptic\nreligious text has at its head the words [Coptic], with God, generally\naccompanied by the so-called Coptic or Orbed Cross, itself an adaptation\nof the _ankh_ or symbol of life in Pagan Egypt. That this was the\npractice with heretics as well as orthodox Christians is shown by the\n_Bruce Papyrus_, which actually bears as its frontispiece such words and\nsuch a cross with the letters Α and Ω and which seems to be a\nreproduction of the Constantinian Labarum.[43] If, too, we put side by\nside the passages in our MS. and the _Bruce Papyrus_ which are\npractically identical—as is the case with the three sacraments or\nbaptisms mentioned in the Fourth Document of our text—we find that the\n“seals” or diagrams, passwords, and names given in the Oxford MS. have\nall been omitted from the London book. No one who is familiar with the\nbeliefs current in Pagan Egypt can mistake the reason of this omission,\nwhich is obviously to avoid the risk of their being used in magic.[44] A\nlike precaution was taken with many chapters of the _Book of the Dead_\nand becomes more insistent with every successive recension. It is absent\nfrom the Pyramid texts, doubtless because when these were once carved on\nthe inside of a royal burying-place and the entrance closed, there was\nlittle risk of these being seen by unauthorised persons. The same reason\ndoubtless operated in the same way with the wooden coffins of the\neleventh dynasty on which the next recension was inscribed. But with the\nTheban recension of the New Empire, the case was changed. “Let no one\noutside know it. It is a mystery which is not known to the common\npeople,” says the hundred and sixty-first chapter after directions to\nengrave it on the coffin of the dead. “Reveal it not to anyone, may he\nbe thy father or thy son except thyself. It is a real mystery.”[45] So,\ntoo, with the Saite recension. “This book is most secret,” says the\nhundred and sixty-second chapter, which M. Pierret thinks was intended\nto be the last. “Let it not be seen by any man, for it is forbidden to\nknow it. Let it be hidden. It is called the mistress of the hidden\nabode. This is the end.”[46] That similar ideas persisted into Christian\ntimes may be guessed from the Homily _de Magis_ ascribed to St. Ephraim\nin which the Homilist tells his hearers that in his day (circa A.D. 450)\neven the clergy resorted to magicians for these mysterious writings.\n“Instead of the blessings of the Saints,” he says, “they carry about the\nincantations of the magicians, and instead of the Holy Cross, they carry\nthe books of devils ... and a child who knows nothing at all, carries\nabout devil’s names and comes to church.”[47]"
}

  "passage_text": "It was evidently, therefore, for the information of orthodox persons
that our MS. was made, but not for that of the orthodox public
generally, whether clerical or lay. Had it been so, it would have been
weighted with a running commentary casting scorn upon its erroneous
doctrines, or by so-called refutations like those which encumber the
pages of heresiologists such as Irenæus, Hippolytus, and Epiphanius. Had
it been written by an ecclesiastic, moreover, it would certainly have
borne some preface, or colophon, as does the _Philosophumena_, claiming
merit for, and giving the date of the completion of the work.[48] Yet
there is nothing in the present text to show that it was written by an
ecclesiastic of any kind, while it follows from what has been said above
that it was begun by a scribe who took unusual pains to ensure an
accurate copy, and that when he handed over for a time the continuation
of his work to a subordinate, he yet went over and corrected the
latter’s work with as much care as he bestowed upon his own. All this
suggests that it was made for official or judicial use; and the most
reasonable guess is that it was the draft or copy of a legal document
made for the enlightenment of some conciliar, episcopal, or even secular
tribunal concerned in the suppression of heresy, such as the Inquisitors
of the Faith set up by Theodosius. This would solve the problem which
has so vexed the minds of commentators like Prof. Harnack and Dr.
Schmidt as to the occurrence of the colophon “Part of the Books of the
Saviour” at the foot of the Second and Third Documents. It is natural
enough that the second or subaltern scribe, continuing the work of which
only the first part was once thought sufficient, should preface the
continuation by the title “The Second Tome of Pistis Sophia”; but that
as he completed the copying of each subsequent extract stichometrically
arranged, should add the words: “Part of the Books of the Saviour” to
indicate the collection of MSS., probably seized in a raid by the
Imperial authorities on some heretic’s library, from which they were all
taken.

If this be admitted, it certainly alters materially the view which
recent German scholars, following, perhaps, after their manner, the
first German commentator Köstlin, have formed of the whole text, and in
which we might be inclined to acquiesce if we considered it a mere
Encyclopædia or, as Epiphanius calls his own collection, a
“bread-basket,” in which heterogeneous scraps of doctrine were thrown
together anyhow. If, on the other hand, it was made for the use of a
tribunal, it would be in the order of things concerned with the tenets
of one school or sect alone, and this we find on investigation to be the
case. Although the episode of Pistis Sophia comes to a stop about
halfway, she is, as has been said, mentioned in the Fourth Document as
well as in the First and Second, and even in the Third there are phrases
which show that its author has the same general conception of the
constitution of the universe, of the Person and Mission of Jesus, and of
the means of salvation as the writers of the earlier parts. Yet it is
equally plain that no two of the documents are by the same hand. While
the First Document makes the Power which Jesus received from Barbelo
“the body which He wore in the Height,”[49] and His soul another power
received from one of the great leaders of “the Height,”[50] the Second
Document attributes the Incarnation to a lesser power of “the Middle”
who casts what came from the same leader into “the matter of Barbelo,”
which thereupon becomes the earthly and not the heavenly body of the
Saviour.[51] In like manner, while the First Document puts into the
mouth of Mary the Mother a story not traceable to any other source about
the Holy Spirit coming down from the First Mystery in the exact likeness
of Jesus’ earthly body, and says that after kissing each other, they
become one,[52] the Second Document makes St. John say that the First
Mystery himself came down upon Jesus in the form of a dove, but in a
“vesture of light” received from Barbelo.[53] So, again, the First
Document especially declares that “the disciples” (not the Apostles)
were endowed by Jesus at His coming with twelve powers from the
Treasure-house of Light instead of the souls which they would otherwise
have received from the Rulers,[54] while the Second makes Jesus tell
them that their souls instead of coming straight from the Treasure-house
have suffered much from transmigration into different bodies.[55] So,
too, the Sphere of Destiny, which in the First Document is described as
“the Second Sphere”[56] (or the one which is reached from the earth next
after passing through the First Sphere, below which is the visible
firmament), is in the Third Document transformed into a Place called
“Great Destiny,”[57] which is in the Place of the head of the Æons [or
Zodiac] which Place they call “the Place of the Kingdom of Adamas,” the
Ruler of the twelve Æons or signs, and in the Fourth Document is made
equivalent to the Sphere or visible firmament only.[58] And so again
“the cause of sin,” which in the Third Document is laid upon the
shoulders of “the Five Rulers of Great Destiny,”[59] is in the Fourth
assigned to certain demons from the Middle Way who enter into man.[60]
These discrepancies are too great to be accounted for as merely clerical
errors or mistakes in translation, and we can therefore only attribute
them to the different documents being the work of different authors.[61]"

  "passage_text": "This being the case, we must, to get a true perspective of the work,\nseek for the earliest document in it, and then endeavour to arrange the\nothers in their relative order of date; and I have no hesitation in\ndeciding that in this, the scribes followed the usual practice in legal\nmatters and that the earliest document is that which comes first in the\nMS. Not only has it a regular preface, an advantage which it shares with\nthe Fourth, but it is the one of the four principal documents which\nalone gives an orderly and coherent account of the heavenly hierarchy\nand its “Places,”[62] and therefore affords the reader a sort of key to\nthe system of its successors. Hence it must be considered as the mother\ndocument, so to speak, from which all the rest are derived, or to which\nthey refer; and it will be found on examination that while all these\ncontain what may be called supplemental information as to the different\nuniverses or worlds and their inhabitants, there is none which deals so\nexhaustively with the speculations that during the early centuries of\nour Era occupied the attention of orthodox and heretic alike, that is to\nsay, the Constitution of the Godhead and the relation of the Saviour to\nthe Supreme Being. It is also probable that anyone making extracts for\njudicial use from the books of a sect would begin with the most\ninformative; and while Pistis Sophia is here described so fully as to\nleave no doubt in one’s mind that the author knows that he is here\nintroducing her to his readers for the first time, the references to her\nin the other documents are so brief as to show that their writers knew\nthat their readers had already heard about her. But the most conclusive\nproof at present of the anteriority of the First Document as compared\nwith the others, is that it does not quote from the Fourth Gospel. The\nopening words of St. John would have been extremely useful to the author\nin expressing the relations between his Ineffable One and the First\nMystery, and are in fact so used later both in the _Excerpta Theodoti_\nand the _Bruce Papyrus_.[63] Ptolemy and Heracleon,[64] the leaders of\nthe sect to which, as will be shown later, our text can with the\ngreatest likelihood be attributed, both knew of this Gospel and discuss\nits words and especially its opening at length. Yet the author of our\nFirst Document not only makes no use of this, but he gives no quotation\namong the many from the New Testament to be found in this Document that\ncan by any possibility be assigned to the Fourth Gospel, save those\nwhich may equally well be taken from the Synoptics. The one apparent\nexception to this statement is neither conclusive in itself, nor strong\nenough to found any argument upon it.[65] In the later part of the\nSecond Document, however, the words of St. John: “Where I am, there\nshall my servants be,” may possibly be thought to underlie the sentence\nin our text: “Wherefore I said unto you aforetime: Where I shall be,\nthere will be with Me my Twelve servants,”[66] the word διάκονος being\nused in both cases; and in the Fourth Document there appear unmistakably\nthe conversation of Jesus with the Samaritan woman,[67] and the spear\nthrust in His side at the Crucifixion,[68] neither of which incidents\nare recorded in the Synoptics. The conclusion, therefore, seems\nirresistible that while the author of the First Document did not know of\nSt. John’s Gospel, the writer of part of the Second may have done so,\nand the writer of the Fourth was fully acquainted with it.\n\nYet the literary critic, especially he who is acquainted with the\nliterature of the early Christian centuries, will hardly require further\nproof of the relative dates of our four chief Documents than that\nafforded by a comparison of their contents. In the First, apart from a\nsketch of—to use a comprehensive word—the uranography of the sect, and\nthe speculations about the Divine Nature before referred to, the author\ndevotes nearly all his space to the episode of Pistis Sophia, which may\nfairly be looked upon as an allegory pointing out to man the penalty of\ntransgressing the Divine Law, and the necessity of repentance. Thus, in\none of the “Penitences” addressed to the highest Power that she knew,\nPistis Sophia confesses that she has offended “the Law of the Light” and\nattributes her deliverance from Chaos to her consequent repentance.[69]\nThere is more than one hint in the text that both the fall and the\nrepentance take place within what is called “the world of humanity,” and\nwe can without any overstraining of the allegory consider Pistis Sophia\nas representing the heathen world before the light of Christianity\nraised it from the degradation into which it had fallen by its material\nluxury, and restored it to something like what was supposed to be its\nprimeval innocence.[70] Hence we have a fairly close parallel to stories\nlike that of Christian in the _Pilgrim’s Progress_, who leaves the city\nof Mansoul to strive upward to the Heavenly City; and allowing for the\ndifference of time and place, there is no reason why we should consider\nthe Coptic version as the more ignoble allegory of the two. It should\nalso be noticed that in this Document, the terrors of hell are hardly\ntouched upon, and the “afflictions” of Sophia are spoken of throughout\nas confined to the loss of “light” and her consequent impotence to\nreturn without Divine aid to the Place which she had wilfully abandoned.\nLastly magic and astrology are expressly if briefly condemned as\nunlawful knowledge brought to men by the sinning angels."

The author of the Second Document,\nafter making a somewhat clumsy effort to conclude the history of Pistis\nSophia, does not, as we might expect him to do, continue the account of\nJesus’ upward journey, but dismisses it to plunge into a series of\ninquiries as to the exact nature of the heavenly hierarchies and the\namount of “Light” which each of them enjoys; and the answers of the\nSaviour not only describe these at great length, but indicate, though\nobscurely, the various steps by which man can approach divinity. But the\nbenefits there promised are to be confined evidently to a small and\nprivileged class chosen out of the main body of Christians. The use of\nthese means, moreover, is a good deal more magical than religious—that\nis to say, they apparently act by compulsion rather than by propitiation\nof the celestial powers—and was perhaps bound up with the different\n“arrays” of stars in a fashion which shows a distinct leaning towards\nthe astrology of the time.[71] The rebel Rulers of the stars are here\nmade for the first time the instruments in the punishment of sinful\nsouls,[72] and the terrors of hell are held out as a menace which may\ninduce mankind to accept initiation into the mysteries offered. In all\nthis, we cannot but see the reversion to Pagan practices, to the\ndualistic theory of the universe, and to the tendency to appeal to\nignoble motives into which post-Christian gnosticism sank in its\ndecadence, and which finds, perhaps, its fullest expression in\nManichaeism.\n\nThe Interpolated Fragment is, it is true, markedly free from these\nobjections. The gaze of the author of this is indeed turned upwards\ninstead of downwards, and we find him indulging in unrestrained\nspeculation as to the “members” of the Supreme Being which are still\nunmanifested but existed before even the First Mystery, and have\napparently remained without emanation.[73] The fragment is too short for\nus to guess of what practical use these pretended revelations are\nsupposed to be; but Jesus is represented as saying with regard to the\n“Members,” that “He is the Treasure-house of them all.” Something of the\nkind is hinted at in the long catalogue of transcendental powers given\nin the Second Document; and it is therefore possible that this Fragment\nmay once have formed part of some continuation of the account of Jesus’\njourney upwards which was in course of narration when broken off to\nrecount the episode of Pistis Sophia.\n\nThe Third Document, however, resumes the descent of the slope of\ndegradation with increased speed. As with the Egyptian funerary texts\nwhich succeeded and in some measure supplanted the _Book of the\nDead_,[74] the punishments after death and the way to escape them form\nthe principal theme of this Document. As for magic, the gifts of healing\nand working of miracles, here explained as the raising of the dead and\nthe casting out of devils, which the Epistle to the Corinthians puts\namong the Charismata or gifts of the Spirit,[75] are here said to belong\nto the Rulers or wicked Archons, and to be only lawfully exercised by\nthe disciples for the purpose of spreading the faith throughout the\nworld.[76] So, too, the information as to the fourfold division of man’s\nincorporeal part: Power, Soul, Spirit Counterfeit, and Fate, is all\ntaken from the popular beliefs of Pagan Egypt; and the formulas enabling\nthe initiate to “loose the bonds” which bind the soul to the worst of\nthese, are as clearly to be referred to the belief in the power of names\nand in the compulsion of the spirit-world which Iamblichus tells us was\nthe main peculiarity of Egyptian magic.[77] The divisions of the place\nof punishment into four hells of graduated intensity and the final doom\nof annihilation for the worst sinners are also taken from the same\nliterature.[78] So far does this go, that even the uninitiated dead when\nin the worst of all the hells can escape from his torments and enjoy a\nqualified beatitude, if he then repeats certain names which he has\nlearned during his life.[79] It is quite true that we hear in this\nDocument about the Love of God and the initiates doing things worthy of\nthe mysteries and praying prayers in certain forms; but its general\ntendency remains almost entirely magical."
}

  "passage_text": "With the Fourth Document, we seem to have reached the bottom of the\nslope. The disciples here know nothing—it will be remembered that the\nscene is supposed to take place directly after the Resurrection—of the\nhigher worlds and their mysteries, or even of the parts of this Chorema\nor Space which are above the Treasure-house; and their flight upward\nwith Jesus has for its object merely the exhibition of the terrors of\none of the Places of Punishment. So, too, the information which they\nobtain both by sight and by word of mouth as to the disposition and\nnames of the stars and planets can hardly have been of use to them\nexcept for the purpose of magic and astrology. Of the joys prepared for\nthe faithful and of the glories of the Divine Presence described in the\n_Book of Enoch_ and other Apocrypha, they are told nothing. The\nsacraments that Jesus celebrates for them are, it would seem, to be\ngiven to them in return for leaving all and following Him;[80] but are\nentirely magical in character, and nothing is said of any abandonment of\nsinful practices or of any repentance being necessary for their\nefficacy. The sign that He asks for from His Father,[81] here called\nmerely the Father of the Treasure-house, although not here specifically\ndescribed, is, as we know from the parallel passage in the _Bruce\nPapyrus_, the conversion of the wine in one of the wine-cups into the\n“water of baptism,”[82] in a way which strongly reminds us of the\njuggling sacraments attributed by Irenæus and the other heresiologists\nto the magician Marcus. The formal remission of sins which precedes this\nsacrament is accomplished by the invocation of many powers with\nincomprehensible names, and, if we read the passage correctly, only\nextends to sins of the flesh.[83] They are told to “hide this mystery\nand give it to none” save those who observe His commandments in words\nwhich almost repeat those of the _Book of the Dead_.[84] Yet even these\nsacraments would appear not to be needed by those who know the Great\nName, the utterance of which will put to flight all demons, dissolve\ntheir houses of torment, and subjugate the highest material powers of\nthe universe.[85] Nothing is wanting to show that the sect which put\nforth this Document had slipped back into the preoccupation with the\nterrors of hell which is the prevailing feature of the Egyptian religion\nof the last native dynasties,[86] and that the belief in magic and\nastrology into which Hellenic Paganism had sunk during the third and\nfourth centuries had taken the place of the loftier if vain speculations\nof the earlier Documents of our text. So much is this the case that the\nIneffable One and the First Mystery of the first three Documents are not\neven mentioned here, and the only link connecting this with the story of\nPistis Sophia is the casual mention of her name as supplying a “Power”\nfor the planet Venus.[87]\n\nWith the Fifth Document a still lower level is reached. Hell and its\ntorments form the only subject of this book, which as has been said\nabove, is probably nearly complete, only a few pages of the conclusion\nbeing beyond recall. More proper-names of fiends are given here than in\nany of the preceding documents; and as has been said, these now include\nmany of the Pagan gods such as the Egyptian Typhon, the Syrian Adonis,\nand the Greek Persephone and Hecate. These may possibly have been\nincluded among the subordinate “gods” several times referred to in the\nFirst Document, but the fact that their names are here openly given,\nseems to point to a time when the Pagans were in a minority in the\nEastern world. The increasing influence of the belief in astrology with\nwhich even the Neo-Platonists of Alexandria did not disdain to meddle,\nis also shown by the answer already mentioned of Jesus to an inquiry of\nMary Magdalene wherein He tells her that the allotment of souls to\n“righteous” and “wicked” bodies respectively is periodic and depends\nwholly on the disposition of the stars.\n\nThe bearing that all this has on the absolute as distinct from the\nrelative dating of the five Documents will be dealt with presently.\n\n              4. THE AUTHORSHIP AND DATE OF THE DOCUMENTS"
}
